title: Case–control Xenium: from cells to biology
text:
Workshop Overview
Xenium spatial transcriptomics measures targeted gene expression at single-cell resolution while preserving the physical organization of the tissue. This makes it possible to study which cell populations are present, what genes they express, and where they are located. In case–control human brain data, however, the challenge is not simply to generate clusters: cell identities must be supported by marker genes and reference data, and disease comparisons must respect the donor as the biological replicate.
In this workshop, participants will analyze Xenium data from the human dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, comparing schizophrenia and neurotypical control donors. Working in R and Google Colab with Seurat, participants will start from a prepared object after quality control, normalization, and scaling. They will move step by step through dimensionality reduction, clustering, marker-based cell-type annotation, comparison with a published human DLPFC single-nucleus reference, visualization of annotated cells in tissue space, donor-level cell-type composition, and cell-type-specific pseudobulk differential expression.
By the end of the workshop, participants will be able to explore a single-cell spatial object, cluster cells and interpret a UMAP, annotate broad brain cell types using multiple sources of evidence, map annotations back into tissue space, compare cell-type proportions between groups, and perform donor-aware differential expression. Throughout the analysis, emphasis is placed on avoiding pseudoreplication, recognizing the limitations of a targeted 300-gene panel, and separating exploratory teaching results from publication-level biological conclusions.

title: Mapping Biology in Space — DBiT-seq and the Basics of Spatial Multi-Omics Analysis
text:
Workshop Overview
Sequencing tells you what molecules are present in a sample; it rarely tells you where. Bulk sequencing averages an entire tissue into one profile, and single-cell sequencing resolves individual cells only by dissociating the tissue and destroying their spatial context. Spatial multi-omics closes that gap: it keeps each molecular readout pinned to its original (x, y) position in the tissue.
This session introduces spatial multi-omics analysis through DBiT-seq (Deterministic Barcoding in Tissue), a microfluidic method that stamps a barcode grid directly onto a tissue section. Two perpendicular sets of channels tag every pixel with a unique barcode combination, so RNA, chromatin accessibility (ATAC), and protein (via antibody-derived tags) can all be measured on the same pixels of the same section — three molecular layers, one spatial grid.
Participants work hands-on in a browser-based notebook (no installation required) with a real published dataset: a P21 mouse brain profiled by spatial ARP-seq (ATAC + RNA + Protein) from Zhang et al., Nature 647, 213–227 (2025). No programming background is assumed — most cells are pre-written and simply run and read; a handful of “Your turn” cells invite participants to change one value and observe the effect.

title: Mapping Biology in Space — DBiT-seq and the Basics of Spatial Multi-Omics Analysis
text:
What the session covers

Why spatial multi-omics — how it differs from bulk and single-cell sequencing, and where DBiT-seq sits relative to other platforms (e.g., Visium HD, spatial ATAC-seq).
Reading the figures — how to interpret the chart types common to omics papers: bar plots, heatmaps, dot plots, and GO/KEGG enrichment as bubble plots or networks.
The tissue and the study — mouse cortical anatomy at postnatal day 21 (layered neurons, the myelinating corpus callosum) and what the source paper found: cortical layers sharpen and the corpus callosum myelinates over development, with chromatin accessibility changes preceding transcriptional changes at the same loci.
Hands-on analysis — loading and aligning the three molecular tables to a shared pixel grid, checking tissue orientation, visualizing RNA/ATAC/protein signal for the same gene, handling sparse ATAC signal by aggregating gene programmes, and normalizing each modality.
Validation — plotting a panel of known cortical-layer marker genes (Cux2, Rasgrf2, Rorb, Bcl11b, Foxp2, Tle4, Mbp, Plp1) and checking that they land in the expected anatomical layers, as the criterion for trusting the rest of the analysis.

title: Mapping Biology in Space — DBiT-seq and the Basics of Spatial Multi-Omics Analysis
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of the session, participants should be able to:

Explain what spatial multi-omics adds over bulk and single-cell sequencing.
Describe how DBiT-seq co-registers RNA, ATAC, and protein measurements to the same tissue pixels.
Read and interpret the standard chart types used to report omics results.
Load, align, and visualize multi-modal spatial data in a shared coordinate system.
Use known anatomical markers to validate that a spatial dataset is correctly oriented and biologically sound before drawing further conclusions.

title: Mapping Biology in Space — DBiT-seq and the Basics of Spatial Multi-Omics Analysis
text:
Format
Self-paced, browser-based (Google Colab), roughly following five blocks: environment setup, why spatial multi-omics, reading the figures, the tissue and the study, and hands-on analysis with validation. Demonstrators are available throughout for troubleshooting.

title: MERFISH: whole-embryo spatial transcriptomics
text:
Workshop Overview
Most spatial transcriptomics methods require thin sections. MERFISH, applied to whole mounts, does not: it resolves individual mRNA molecules in three dimensions inside an intact embryo. In this session we work with weMERFISH data — 495 genes imaged at subcellular resolution in whole zebrafish embryos across gastrulation and early organogenesis — and ask what becomes possible once every cell keeps its address.
The session is built around a single notebook, run on the local HIVE server (installed by Bruker for the Summer School). No personal laptop setup and no prior Python is assumed, though you will get more out of it if you have seen scanpy before.






Run the notebook — on the HIVE server




In D:\Students, create a folder with your name or nickname.
Copy the file 2026V4SDBSummerSchool-MERFISH_Archive/01_weMERFISH_basics_YW_updated1 into that folder.
Open the file.
If VS Code opens it in Restricted Mode, click Manage → Trust the folder.
Open the Extensions panel (left-hand sidebar) and install the Jupyter extension.
Click Run All. When prompted to pick a kernel, choose the V4SDB Python environment.
Enjoy the ride.









Nothing to download



The two embryo files the notebook needs are already provided on the HIVE server — nothing to download from Dryad, and no internet connection is required during the session.

title: MERFISH: whole-embryo spatial transcriptomics
text:
Software
We use the standard scverse Python stack: scanpy, leidenalg, igraph, requests, plotly, nbformat. On the HIVE server these are already installed in the V4SDB Python environment you select when you run the notebook, so the notebook’s own pip install cell should not need to do any real work — it is there mainly for anyone later running the notebook outside the HIVE server.
scanpy

The general-purpose single-cell analysis toolkit. The same library you will have used for 10x data — which is exactly the point. Its native sc.pl.spatial() function does most of the plotting here.

AnnData

The container format. Cells × genes, plus annotations on both axes and arbitrary matrices attached to each.

squidpy

Spatial extensions to scanpy: neighbourhood enrichment, spatial statistics, image handling. Not required for this session but the natural next step.

plotly

Used for the interactive 3D embryo view.

title: MERFISH: whole-embryo spatial transcriptomics
text:
Data
Wan Y, El Kholtei J, Jenie I, et al. (2026) Whole-embryo spatial transcriptomics at subcellular resolution from gastrulation to organogenesis. Science. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.adt3439
The full dataset is deposited at Dryad under doi:10.5061/dryad.j0zpc86v9 (129 GB, CC0). We only ever need two files from it — the 50% and 75% epiboly embryos — which are provided directly on the HIVE server rather than fetched live from Dryad during the session.
The atlas can also be browsed interactively at MERFISHEYES, and the analysis code from the paper is at github.com/yinan-wan0/weMERFISH.

title: MERFISH: whole-embryo spatial transcriptomics
text:
Workshop step by step

0. Setup
Confirm the packages are available (already true in the V4SDB environment on the HIVE server), then point the notebook at the two embryo .h5ad files.


1. A quick tour of the weMERFISH AnnData object
Reading .h5ad into AnnData and finding your way around it: cell metadata, the gene panel, and — the field that matters most for a whole-mount dataset — the spatial coordinates, which live in .obsm['spatial'] for every stage.


2. QC and data preparation
The distributed files have already passed the authors’ own QC and filtering, so we don’t re-run a 10x-style filtering pipeline. What we do look at: counts and detected genes per cell, and — the diagnostic unique to spatial data — whether a cluster holds together in physical space, not just in expression space.


3. Plotting the embryo in space
The native imaging-space view via sc.pl.spatial(), alongside the precomputed spherical sphere_side / sphere_top views, plus an interactive, rotatable 3D scatter of the whole embryo.


4. Gene expression in space
Mapping individual genes onto the embryo surface. Reading the BMP/Chordin dorsoventral gradient (bmp4 vs chrd) directly off the data.


5. Clustering and spatial structure
The familiar PCA–neighbours–Leiden workflow run on the full 495-gene panel. Then the question that only spatial data permits: put clusters computed without any coordinate information back onto the embryo and ask whether they correspond to real tissue domains, alongside a confusion matrix against the authors’ own annotation and a standard marker-gene analysis.


6. Comparing across stages
Loading the 75% epiboly embryo and comparing one gene — tbxta — between stages, both as spatial maps and as a quantitative profile along the animal–vegetal axis. A prompt to think about the limits of comparing snapshots rather than tracked cells.

Training materials for the 2026 V4SDB Student Summer School
Instructor:
Sergio Marco Salas (KTH Royal Institute of Technology, Stockholm)
sergiomarco.salas@scilifelab.se

title: Image-Based Spatial Transcriptomics: From Segmentation to Domains
text:
Workshop Overview
Building on the foundational workshop on image-based spatial transcriptomics by Katarina Dragicevic and Dorottya Ralbovszki, this session deepens hands-on experience using Xenium samples from the human dorsal striatum. While standard transcriptomic analysis focuses primarily on cell-type identification, capturing true tissue architecture requires integrating physical coordinates, cell morphology, and localized microenvironments.
Working in Python within the scverse ecosystem (utilizing libraries such as Scanpy, Squidpy, and SpatialData), participants will explore complementary spatial workflows. The hands-on pipeline moves step-by-step through evaluating and refining cell segmentation, performing spatial domain identification (niche clustering), and calculating spatial statistics to quantify cell–cell co-localization, spatial autocorrelation, and neighborhood enrichment patterns within the striatal tissue.
By the end of the workshop, participants will be able to:

Navigate and manipulate spatial transcriptomics objects natively in Python.
Critically evaluate image-based cell segmentation boundaries and transcript assignment.
Identify and visualize distinct spatial domains and tissue microenvironments.
Calculate quantitative spatial statistics to test hypotheses about cellular distribution.

Throughout the session, emphasis is placed on understanding the computational assumptions behind cell segmentation algorithms, choosing appropriate spatial neighborhood graphs, and applying best practices in Python for downstream spatial data interpretation.

title: Visium spatial transcriptomics (heart sections)
text:
Workshop Overview
In developmental biology, spatial transcriptomics allows researchers to measure gene expression while preserving the tissue’s spatial organization, revealing how cell types and gene programs are arranged across an organ as it forms. However, working with spatial data introduces challenges not present in standard single-cell analysis: each measurement reflects a mixture of cells at a fixed position, and deciding what signal to keep versus filter out is a central part of the analysis. This workshop aims to demonstrate the effective utilization of 10x Genomics Visium data through hands-on analysis of embryonic heart sections. Participants will work step by step through loading, filtering, processing, and clustering spatial transcriptomics data in R using the semla and Seurat packages, first on a single tissue section and then across three sections spanning different developmental ages, drawing on data from a published atlas of the developing human heart.
By the end of this workshop, participants will be familiar with loading and visualizing Visium data, will have filtered and clustered spots into biologically meaningful groups and mapped them onto tissue anatomy, and will know how to identify cluster-defining genes, correct for batch effects across multiple sections, and explore how gene expression changes across developmental stages.
